title: Minimal N-hydroxyphthalimide-urethane bonds enable superior thermomechanical stability for covalent adaptable networks

paper_content.abstract: Compared to classic thermosets, the reprocessability of covalent adaptable networks (CANs) endowed by dynamic covalent bonds (DCBs) often comes at the expense of mechanical performance and thermomechanical stability. Herein, we report a “High Activity & Low Content” strategy for CANs to achieve superior thermomechanical stability, which is enabled by dynamic N-hydroxyphthalimide-urethane bonds (NUBs). The catalyst-free addition reaction between N-hydroxyphthalimides and isocyanates proceeds to an near-quantitative conversion within 2 h at room temperature in dimethyl sulfoxide, while the formed bonds dissociate even up to ~28% at 120 °C. The dual high activity, characterized by a high degree of dissociation and fast association kinetics, allows for an effective reduction in DCB content within CANs while preserving their dynamic characteristics. We incorporate only 5 mol% of dynamic units to develop poly(N-hydroxyphthalimide-urethanes) (PNU) networks. The “High Activity & Low Content” design endows PNUs with superior mechanical properties, exceptional crack tolerance, and remarkable mechanical stability at high temperatures. Furthermore, even with minimal DCB participation, the PNUs exhibit excellent reprocessability and mild degradability in neutral aqueous conditions. This study proposes a compelling strategy that enables CANs to achieve excellent reprocessability while retaining their mechanical strength and thermomechanical robustness—overcoming the traditional trade-off between these properties.
paper_content.introduction:
Thermosets with permanently crosslinked structures exhibit mechanical strength, solvent resistance, and durability, but also raise significant sustainability concerns1. Recent studies have reported innovative strategies to convert thermosets into reprocessable covalent adaptable networks (CANs) by incorporating dynamic covalent bonds (DCBs) such as transalkylation2,3, aza-Michael addition4, radical-mediated reaction5, disulfide/diselenide6, C=C/C=N metathesis7,8, nucleophilic aromatic substitution9. However, the developed CAN systems often face a fundamental trade-off: insufficient network dynamics reduce reprocessability, whereas excessive bond exchange degrades mechanical properties, especially the thermomechanical stability10–14. Consequently, it is a significant scientific challenge and practical imperative to pursue a delicate balance between mechanical stability and dynamic adaptability for the design of high-performance CANs.

The macroscopic behaviors of CANs are derived from the thermodynamic and kinetic parameters of DCBs governing the reconfiguration process and the mean lifetime of network crosslinks, as well as the macromolecular topology15–17. To avoid excessive flow of CANs at high temperatures, chemical approaches typically involve tailoring the kinetics of DCBs through trapping reactive counterparts18, developing DCBs with high activation energy barriers14, or introducing multiple types of dynamic bonds with disparate lifetimes, etc16,19–21. In parallel, topological design strategies include tuning cross-linking density22,23, and manipulating phase separation or nanoscale domains24,25 to optimize the balance between mechanical robustness and creep. Despite these significant advancements, most existing studies primarily focus on the service performance of CANs at low temperatures, where dynamic exchange reactions are sluggish or kinetically suppressed by limited polymer chain motion (<Tg or Tm)13,14,26. However, for demanding applications subject to high temperatures, such as thermal insulation and sealing, mechanical stability at elevated temperatures is important. We propose that a more general and straightforward strategy is to minimize the incorporation of dynamic bonds to mitigate the detrimental effects on material properties while enabling the reprocessing of as-formed CANs. For this purpose, DCBs must be carefully designed to satisfy two critical criteria: (i) efficient thermal dissociation (large dissociation equilibrium constant, Kd) at elevated temperatures to facilitate reprocessing, and (ii) rapid association reaction kinetics (large association rate constant, ka) at low temperatures to ensure complete network reformation at low DCB content (Fig. 1).

Reversible isocyanate chemistry, which focuses on the inherent reversibility of urethane/urea bonds, has garnered particular attention due to the diverse substrate structures available for modulating their dynamics1,27–31. This feature provides a promising candidate to meet the abovementioned stringent requirements. Isocyanates are highly reactive and usually react with active hydrogen compounds rapidly (large ka), which is typically accompanied by a substantial enthalpy change (large |ΔH|). Nevertheless, this usually results in a low degree of dissociation (low Kd, Fig. 1) at elevated temperatures27,32,33, as enthalpy changes typically dominate the overall Gibbs free energy change of a reaction. Therefore, developing a reversible chemistry that simultaneously exhibits both large Kd and ka remains challenging15,34.

Herein, we report a type of reversible isocyanate chemistry, N-hydroxyphthalimide-urethane bonds (NUBs), which enable concurrent high dissociability and fast reformation kinetics and demonstrate their efficacy in minimizing DCB content to enhance the mechanical properties and thermomechanical stability of the corresponding CANs. The dynamic chemistry of NUBs is controlled by the electronic effects of the phthalimide moiety in urethane. Specifically, the strong electron-withdrawing capability of the N-hydroxyphthalimide (NHPI) structure renders it a good leaving group5, thus promoting NUB dissociation with a conversion far higher than those of previously reported reversible isocyanate chemistry27,32,33. The high reactivity with isocyanates originates from the unique dipolar tautomer of NHPI, contributing to lowering the transition state activation energy. As a proof-of-concept, we have developed a series of poly(N-hydroxyphthalimide-urethanes) (PNUs) with a minimal proportion of NUBs (5 mol% of the total diisocyanate) as the dynamic building blocks. The resulting PNUs exhibit extraordinary tensile strength, toughness, and resistance to crack propagation, attributable to the reduction of dynamic weak bonds. This “High Activity & Low Content” design ensures thermal reprocessability and mild degradation while effectively maintaining thermomechanical stability of PNUs, as evidenced by excellent dimensional persistence, stress relaxation resistance, and network integrity at elevated temperatures. Consequently, the PNUs demonstrate significant potential as sustainable alternatives to conventional PUs, and this work provides a robust framework for manufacturing high-performance CANs by dynamic chemical design to overcome the traditional trade-off in dynamic networks.
paper_content.results:
Molecular dynamic chemistry
We first synthesized a series of model compounds (Supplementary Figs. S1–7, S37–48). The kinetics of the addition reaction between methoxy-NHPI(1) and hexyl isocyanate were investigated using in situ Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR). The sharp drop of the characteristic peak at 2276 cm–1, corresponding to the asymmetric stretching of the NCO group, implies the rapid formation of N-hydroxyphthalimide-urethane bonds in the absence of a catalyst (Fig. 2a, b). The formation reaction of NUBs exhibits first-order kinetics for both N-hydroxyl compounds and isocyanates (rate = ka[NOH][NCO]) (Supplementary Fig. S8), achieving ~ 97% conversion after approximately 2 h at room temperature with a large association rate constant of 1.3 × 10–2 M–1·s–1 in dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO). The association rate constant ka is comparable to previously reported oxime-urethane and pyrazole-urea bonds32,33. Interestingly, the reaction rate in N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF) dramatically decreased, but it is still much faster than that of conventional uncatalyzed urethane and thiourethane bonds (Fig. 2c and Supplementary Fig. S9)32,35. This phenomenon implies a distinct reaction mechanism for NUBs, since previously reported reversible isocyanate chemistries exhibit comparable reaction kinetics in these two solvents due to their similar hydrogen bonding abilities30,32,36.

Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were conducted to elucidate the mechanism of the addition reaction. The results revealed that NHPI can undergo an intramolecular 1,4-proton transfer (TS1) to form the 1,3-dipolar nitrone isomer (INT1), with an activation energy barrier of 20.5 kcal mol–1 (endergonic by 19.9 kcal mol–1). The nitrone subsequently may react with isocyanate via either a concerted or a stepwise mechanism. The concerted pathway begins with the formation of an isocyanate-nitrone complex (endergonic by 5.2 kcal mol–1) and is featured by the simultaneous hydrogen transfer and nucleophilic attack via a seven-membered ring transition state (TS2, ΔG≠=10.2 kcal mol–1), ultimately yielding the final product (endergonic by 24.1 kcal mol–1). The stepwise pathway in which nucleophilic attack precedes proton transfer is energetically unfavorable because the activation energy is approximately 12.2 kcal mol–1 higher than that of the concerted process. Additionally, theoretical calculations were performed for the direct addition between N-hydroxy and isocyanate via a concerted four-membered ring transition state, analogous to the typical reaction mechanism of isocyanates with alcohols. This pathway is ruled out for the disfavored activation energy barrier as high as 32.8 kcal mol–1 (Fig. 2d and Supplementary Figs. S10, S11). It’s worth noting that the favored reaction mechanism involves a thermodynamically unstable key intermediate, the 1,3-dipolar nitrone tautomer. Given that dipolar isomers (e.g., nitrones) typically exhibit enhanced stability in highly polar solvents (those with large dielectric constants (ε), like DMSO) due to the effective solvation and stabilization of the separated charges via dipole-dipole or ion-dipole interactions, this finding accounts for the remarkably accelerated reaction kinetics we observed in the order of DMSO > DMF > 1, 4-dioxane (εDMSO = 45 > εDMF = 36 > ε1,4-dioxane = 2)37,38.

Thermodynamic studies using in situ variable-temperature 1H NMR revealed that the NUB dissociated to NHPIs and isocyanates at elevated temperatures (Fig. 2e, f). The dissociation reaction reached equilibrium very rapidly in less than 20 min at 80 °C (Supplementary Figs. S12, S13). At 120 °C, the thermal dissociation ratio of NUB was up to 28%, with a dissociation equilibrium constant Kd of 2.72 × 10–2 M (Fig. 2f and Supplementary Table S1). Compared to oxime-urethane (Kd = 3.2 × 10–3 M), pyrazole-urea (Kd = 2.6 × 10–3 M), and imidazole-urea (Kd = 6.2 × 10–3 M, estimated by the Van’t Hoff equation)27,32,33, the dissociation ratio of the NUB endowed by the stronger electron-withdrawing NHPI group was much higher at the same temperature. Thermodynamically, the large dissociation equilibrium constant Kd is attributed to the small enthalpy change (ΔHd = 10.8 ± 0.7 kcal mol–1 from the Van’t Hoff plot) of the dissociation reaction (Fig. 2g, h). Subsequently, the reorganization was proved by the reversible recombination of the dissociated counterparts. When two model compounds, AB and CD, were mixed in anhydrous acetonitrile and heated at 80 °C, as expected, the formed exchange products CB and AD were successfully identified at about 10 min and 12 min by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) (Fig. 2i and Supplementary Fig. S14). Overall, these results demonstrate that the dynamic chemistry of NUBs is different from previously reported dynamic chemistry27,32,33,39–41, and is characterized by a high degree of dissociation and a rapid association rate (large Kd and ka, Supplementary Table S2).

Superior mechanical properties
Mechanical robustness is a prerequisite for CANs to meet the requirements of actual applications. Therefore, the mechanical deterioration associated with the incorporation of DCBs should be minimized as much as possible. With this in mind, we employed HDI, BDO as hard segments, PTMEG, Tri-NH2 as soft segments, and only a small amount (5 mol% relative to HDI) of bifunctional dynamic building blocks (Bi-NOH) to prepare a series of PNUs, denoted as PNU-A, PNU-B and PNU-C, with sequentially decreasing hard/soft segment ratios of 13/6.5, 12/7.5, 11/8.5 (Table 1, Figs. 1, 3a and Supplementary Figs. S15, S19, Table S3). Notably, the introduction of Bi-NOH did not significantly compromise the techno-economic feasibility (Supplementary Table S8). Swelling experiments conducted in different solvents verified that the gel fractions of PNUs remain above 95%, suggesting the well-defined crosslinked networks (Supplementary Fig. S20). Remarkably, PNU-A demonstrated a tensile strength of 43.2 ± 4.3 MPa, attaining an extraordinary elongation-at-break of 1891 ± 72% and a toughness of 404.4 MJ m-3, surpassing other covalently crosslinked dynamic PUs reported to date (Fig. 3b, c and Supplementary Fig. S21, Table S9)7–9,22,32,33,42–49. Their characteristic ‘J-shaped’ stress-strain curves indicated the advent of strain-induced crystallization (SIC) during stretching, a pivotal mechanism underpinning elastomer reinforcement. Consequently, the PNUs exhibited a pretty high true stress at break of up to 1.0 GPa, enabling a 5 kg weight to be lifted by 0.1 g PNU-A elastomer (Supplementary Fig. S22). In sequential cyclic tensile tests, the hysteresis loops increased significantly as the applied strain increased, indicating a progressive energy dissipation mechanism (Fig. 3d and Supplementary Fig. S23).

In addition to minimal incorporation of relatively weak NUBs, the aggregated structure of polymers also plays a crucial role in determining PNU performance. The carbonyl (C=O) stretching vibration regions (1800~1600 cm–1) in the FTIR spectra were deconvolved into multiple subpeaks, suggesting the presence of hierarchical hydrogen bonding. Quantitative analysis revealed that the content of hydrogen-bonded C=O in PNU-A was 73%, which is higher than that in PNU-B (69%) and PNU-C (39%) (Fig. 3e and Supplementary Fig. S24, Table S10). As the temperature increased from 30 to 160 °C, the spectral shifts such as ν(C=O), δ(N-H), ν(C-N) and ν(C-O-C) suggested the progressive dissociation of hydrogen bonds, which allows for effective energy dissipation under deformation (Fig. 3f). In situ stretching wide-angle X-ray scattering (WAXS) was performed to shed more light on the polymer morphology evolution during deformation. When unstretched, PNU-A showed concentric circles in the 2D WAXS spectra, typical of amorphous elastomers. As tensile strain increased, the pattern evolved from concentric circles to distinct spots (Fig. 3g and Supplementary Fig. S25). Concurrently, the broad hump in the 1D WAXS spectra became increasingly sharper, signifying enhanced chain alignment and increasingly ordered molecular packing (Fig. 3h). The underlying molecular mechanism involves the controlled release of soft segments composed of polyether chain segments during the initial stages of deformation. At large strains, the hard segments comprising the symmetric structure of HDI and the aromatic planarity of Bi-NOH withstand more stress and gradually align parallel to the tensile direction. This would facilitate crystallization and further reinforce PNUs (Fig. 3i). These evidences provide a mechanistic explanation for the pronounced nonlinear behavior observed in the stress-strain curves.

Exceptional crack tolerance
In addition to their remarkable ductility and toughness, the orientation of the abundant symmetric structure (from HDI) and aromatic planarity (from Bi-NOH) under deformation also empowers PNUs with exceptional crack tolerance. The PNU-A exhibited a fracture energy of 92.1 kJ m–2 (Fig. 4a), and a tear energy up to 460.1 kJ m–2 (Fig. 4b). In puncture resistance experiments, a 0.5 mm-radius needle tip penetrated a 0.2 mm-thick PNU-A film, yielding a puncture force of 13.2 N and a displacement of 11.2 mm (Fig. 4c). In situ stretching SEM was employed to elucidate the microscale crack growth behavior. A controlled displacement (Δd) was incrementally applied to a pre-cracked PNU-A specimen using an in situ stretching stage (Fig. 4d and Supplementary Fig. S26). During the initial deformation, SEM observations revealed rapid crack-tip blunting. As Δd increased, the crack underwent substantially transverse opening rather than propagating through the specimen. Notably, when Δd increased from 4.5 mm to 5.4 mm, the horizontal width at the narrowest section of the specimen decreased by only 0.077 mm, demonstrating strong resistance to crack advancement. At the final deformation stage, the cross-sectional area further decreased, and the specimen could no longer sustain the increasing applied load, triggering rapid flaw initiation and horizontal propagation, and ultimately resulting in catastrophic failure. Analysis of fracture morphology confirmed a significant deviation of the crack trajectory from its initial path (Fig. 4e, f). Digital image correlation (DIC) strain nephograms indicated that crack tip blunting efficiently alleviated stress concentration by redistributing localized stress to the surrounding region. This enabled the polymer chains near the crack tip to experience substantially greater vertical deformation, which activated SIC and led to significant reinforcement along the vertical axis, thereby inducing anisotropy within the material (Fig. 4g–i). Consequently, the crack tip no longer functioned as a stress concentration region in the horizontal direction, as vertical reinforcement effectively suppressed horizontal crack propagation.

Remarkable thermomechanical stability
To systematically investigate the influence of DCB content on the thermomechanical behavior of CANs, we synthesized two dynamic PNUs (PNU-15 mol% and PNU-30 mol%) alongside NUB-free reference thermoset (CPU) and thermoplastic (TPU) controls, all with the same hard/soft segment ratio as PNU-A (Table 1, Fig. 5a and Supplementary Figs. S15, S16, Table S4, S5). Tensile testing showed that the incorporation of NUBs with rigid ring structures endowed PNU-A with superior comprehensive mechanical properties compared to TPU and CPU. However, as the NUB content increased further, the mechanical response of the PNUs markedly changed from strong and tough to soft and weak, indicating that an overabundance of weak NUBs reduced the capacity of PNUs to withstand high loads and resistance to deformation (Fig. 5b).

Then, the mechanical behavior and dynamic properties at elevated temperatures were systematically evaluated. Dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) revealed a similar two-stage thermal transition in the storage modulus (E’), attributable to the distinct thermal transitions of the hard and soft segments. Notably, PNU-A retained a constant modulus plateau in the high-temperature region up to 160 °C, a characteristic also observed in CPU. This behavior suggested that the incorporation of a small fraction (5 mol%) of dynamic units minimally perturbed the integrity of the overall crosslinked network at high temperatures. However, at higher DCB contents, this plateau progressively evolved into a viscous-flow transition similar to TPU, featuring a continuously declining modulus (Fig. 5c, Supplementary Figs. S27, S28 and Table S11, S12). The temperature-strain curves quantitatively corroborated this trend. At lower temperatures, all PNUs deformed slowly with the same temperature dependency. Above 50 °C, however, strain increased suddenly, because of the softening of hard segments and the accelerated dissociation/exchange of DCBs. At 80 °C, the strain of PNU-A reached only ~9.0%, second to CPU (~4.1%), and much lower than PNU-15 mol% (~13.1%) and PNU-30 mol% (~20.9%) (Fig. 5d). Optical images further illustrated the dimensional stability at high temperatures: the triangular geometry of PNU-A was preserved upon heating, whereas PNU-30 mol% underwent pronounced viscous flow (Fig. 5e). Considering their similar transition temperatures from DMA, the poor dimensional stability is mainly due to the significant increase in network plasticity caused by dissociation of excessive DCBs.

The dynamic properties of networks were further studied by temperature-dependent stress relaxation experiments (Fig. 5f, g and Supplementary Fig. S29). As the temperature increased from 120 to 150 °C, the characteristic relaxation time (τ*) of PNU-A decreased from 4049 s to 339 s. In contrast, PNU-15 mol% and PNU-30 mol% exhibited notably shorter τ* even at 80 °C, reflecting accelerated network reorganization with increasing DCB content. In high-temperature time sweeps, PNU-A showed no discernible changes in storage (G’) and loss (G”) moduli over at least 60 min, indicating excellent thermomechanical stability of PNUs upon heating (Fig. 5h). Frequency sweeps revealed that PNU-A maintained a stable crosslinked network, similar to CPU, with its G’ consistently exceeding G” and both moduli remaining temperature-insensitive at 100~140 °C. In contrast, the network of PNU-15 mol% was much more susceptible to heat, resulting in a pronounced reduction in its modulus. Strikingly, PNU-30 mol% displayed a G’/G” crossover at a lower temperature of 100 °C, indicative of a transition to a viscous-flow dominant state (Fig. 5i–k and Supplementary Fig. S30). Additionally, PNUs with a minimal NUBs exhibit comparable hygrothermal aging resistance to the CPU (Supplementary Fig. S31 and Table S13). Taken together, these results fully reflect that the “High Activity & Low Content” design preserves an integrated network with a high-temperature mechanical stability, which is significant for high-temperature applications of CANs, while still enabling dynamic adaptability.

Reprocessability and mild degradability
Arrhenius analysis revealed that the PNUs with varying hard/soft segment ratios exhibited similar stress relaxation activation energies of 23.9~26.9 kcal mol–1, suggesting that the plasticity of these networks is governed by the rearrangement of NUBs. Due to the high dissociation and the rapid reformation of the NUBs, PNUs containing only 5 mol% DCB could be efficiently hot pressed at 140 °C under 10 MPa for 30 min (Fig. 6a, b). Tensile tests revealed that the PNUs containing 5 mol% NUBs retained nearly unchanged tensile strength and elongation at break after repeated reprocessing, whereas both poly(oxime-urethane) (POU) containing 5 mol% oxime-urethane bonds with a relatively low degree of dissociation (12% at 120 °C vs. 28% at 120 °C for NUBs) and CPU (without NUBs) exhibit poor reprocessability and pronounced deterioration due to insufficient topological rearrangement (Table 1, Fig. 6c–e and Supplementary Table S6, Figs. S17, S32, S33). These results demonstrate that our “High activity & Low content” strategy strikes a balance between efficient network rearrangement and mechanical retention.

In addition to thermal reprocessability, we achieved degradation of PNUs under mild natural aqueous conditions and direct reuse of the degradation products. Urethane bonds are intrinsically stable, so the conventional chemical recycling of PU usually requires harsh conditions such as high temperature, acids/bases, or catalysts1,50,51. In contrast, our strategy exploited the high thermal dissociation tendency of NUBs and captured the generated isocyanates with water, thereby irreversibly shifting the equilibrium toward dissociation under mild conditions (Fig. 6f). Model experiments showed that the NUBs dissociated into NHPIs and isocyanates, with the latter subsequently reacting with water to form urea. This process was evidenced by a urea N-H proton appearing at δ 5.73 ppm in the 1H NMR spectrum, alongside an exchangeable proton at δ 10.80 ppm attributable to the N-hydroxy compound. At 100 °C, nearly complete degradation was attained after 8 h (Fig. 6g and Supplementary Fig. S34). Guided by this insight, the linear PNU-D bearing NUBs (Supplementary Fig. S18, Table S7) were prepared and then degraded in DMF containing 10% water at 100 °C. After 3 days, the weight-average molecular weight (Mw) of the PNU-D decreased from 50.0 kDa to 22.2 kDa (Fig. 6h). The resulting oligomers, enriched with polar groups (urea and urethane), were directly repurposed as adhesives. They demonstrated robust adhesion to diverse substrates via hydrogen bonding or coordination interactions (Fig. 6i, j and Supplementary Fig. S35, S36). These investigations provided valuable insights for designing reprocessable and degradable polymers by skillfully employing dual-active NUBs.
paper_content.methods:
Synthesis of the crosslinked PNUs
Typical procedure: polyols (e.g., BDO, PTMEG) were vacuum dehydrated for 12 h before use, and the flasks were dried in a vacuum oven at 120 °C. HDI (10 equiv., 30 mmol, 5.046 g) and Bi-NOH (0.5 equiv., 1.5 mmol, 0.510 g) were dissolved in 30 mL anhydrous DMF, and the mixture was stirred overnight at room temperature under N2 atmosphere. Then PTMEG (5.5 equiv., 16.5 mmol, 16.500 g), BDO (2.5 equiv., 7.5 mmol, 0.676 g), and DBTDL (0.030 g) were added, and the solution was mechanically stirred at 80 °C for 3 h under N2 atmosphere. The reaction system was then diluted with 100 mL anhydrous 1,4-dioxane and cooled to room temperature. Tri-NH2 (1 equiv., 3 mmol, 1.320 g) dissolved in 10 mL anhydrous 1,4-dioxane was slowly added to the reaction solution under vigorous stirring, followed by a rapid increase in viscosity and gelation. The prepared PNU gels were placed in a fume hood to evaporate the solvent at room temperature for 24 h and then placed in a vacuum oven at 60 °C for 12 h to remove the residual solvent.

Synthesis of the reference TPU and CPU
TPU procedure: polyols (e.g., BDO, PTMEG) were vacuum dehydrated for 12 h before use, and the flasks were dried in a vacuum oven at 120 °C. HDI (10 equiv., 30 mmol, 5.046 g), PTMEG (7 equiv., 21 mmol, 21.000 g), BDO (3 equiv., 9 mmol, 0.811 g), and DBTDL (0.030 g) were dissolved in 30 mL anhydrous DMF, and the mixture was mechanically stirred at 80 °C for 3 h under N2 atmosphere. The prepared TPU was placed in a fume hood to evaporate the solvent at room temperature for 24 h and then placed in a vacuum oven at 60 °C for 12 h to remove the residual solvent.

CPU procedure: polyols (e.g., BDO, PTMEG) were vacuum dehydrated for 12 h before use, and the flasks were dried in a vacuum oven at 120 °C. HDI (10 equiv., 30 mmol, 5.046 g), PTMEG (5.5 equiv., 16.5 mmol, 16.500 g), BDO (3 equiv., 9 mmol, 0.811 g,) and DBTDL (0.030 g) were dissolved in 30 mL anhydrous DMF, and the mixture was mechanically stirred at 80 °C for 3 h under N2 atmosphere. The reaction system was then diluted with 100 mL anhydrous 1,4-dioxane and cooled to room temperature. Tri-NH2 (1 equiv., 3 mmol, 1.320 g) dissolved in 10 mL anhydrous 1,4-dioxane was slowly added to the reaction solution under vigorous stirring, followed by a rapid increase in viscosity and gelation. The prepared CPU gel was placed in a fume hood to evaporate the solvent at room temperature for 24 h and then placed in a vacuum oven at 60 °C for 12 h to remove the residual solvent.

Synthesis of the reference POU
The synthesis procedure for POU was analogous to that for crosslinked PNUs. In the formulation, Bi-NOH (0.5 equiv., 1.5 mmol, 0.510 g) was replaced by dimethylglyoxime (0.5 equiv., 1.5 mmol, 0.174). All other steps remained identical.

Synthesis of the linear PNU (PNU-D)
PEG was vacuum dehydrated for 12 h before use, and the flasks were dried in a vacuum oven at 120 °C. HDI (10 equiv., 30 mmol, 5.046 g) and Bi-NOH (1 equiv., 3 mmol, 1.021 g) were dissolved in 30 mL anhydrous DMF, and the sealed mixture was stirred overnight at room temperature. After adding PEG (9 equiv., 27 mmol, 27.000 g) and DBTDL (0.030 g), the solution was mechanically stirred at 80 °C for 3 h under a N2 atmosphere.

Reprocessing of the crosslinked PUs
Reprocessing experiments were carried out by hot pressing. The specimens were sectioned into small pieces and subsequently hot pressed within a rectangular mold at 120 °C or 140 °C under 10 MPa for 30 min. After cooling to room temperature, the reprocessed samples (recycle 1) were demolded and then cut into dumbbell-shaped specimens for uniaxial tensile measurements, as well as rectangular specimens for DMA. The recycle 1 specimens were reprocessed repeatedly following the abovementioned procedure to obtain recycle 2, recycle 3, and recycle 4 specimens, respectively.

Mild degradation of PNU-D
The chemical degradation mechanism of NUBs was investigated by 1H NMR using the model compound (CD). CD (0.384 g, 1.2 mmol) and 324 µL of H2O (18 mmol) were added into DMSO-d6 to prepare a 0.2 M solution. The mixture was then stirred at different temperatures, and samples were taken out at different periods for 1H NMR (Supplementary Fig. S21). Upon heating, CD dissociated into 1 and 2, and the latter reacted irreversibly with water to form the transient 3, which was consumed by the next dissociated 2 to form 4 with a urea structure, contributing to a continuous shift of the chemical equilibrium of CD in the direction of dissociation. The percentage of degradation was determined by the integral ratio of b (belonging to the starting compound CD) and b’ (belonging to the degradation product 4).

We then investigated the degradation of PNU-D bearing the NUBs (Supplementary Table S6). A DMF solution (containing 10% water) of PNU-D was stirred at 100 °C, and samples were taken out at selected times for GPC monitoring of molecular weight change. The resulting oligomers were cast into a film for the next adhesion experiments.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
Zhao et al. reported a “High Activity & Low Content” strategy for CANs to achieve superior thermomechanical stability, which is enabled by a novel type of dynamic N-hydroxyphthalimide-urethane bonds (NUBs). The preparation, dynamic properties, mechanical properties and crack tolerance and recyclability were systematically investigated. Besides, the data were organized very well and the manuscript is well written. Thus, I think this work can be published in Nature communications after minor revisions Some suggestions are as follows.
1. In introduction section: Currently, it gives a broad overview of the challenges in transforming thermoset PUs into CANs, but a more precise statement of the problem, such as the exact limitations of existing strategies in balancing mechanical and re - processing properties, would strengthen the introduction.
2. Although authors used swelling test to prove the network feature of CANs, gel content should be measured to further clearly demonstrate the network integrity of the CANs.
3. Authors used in - situ Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) experiment for studying the addition reaction between methoxy - NHPI and hexyl isocyanate. It’s better to use more experimental techniques to further validate the kinetic of this reaction. For example, differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) could be used to study the thermal behavior during the reaction.
4. To prove the advance of this work, it’s better to include a table or a figure comparing the properties of PNUs with other relevant CANs reported in the literature.
5. Long - term stability tests such as hygrothermal aging resistance should be conducted to assess the durability of PNUs in practical applications.
6. An analysis of the scalability of the synthesis process and an estimate of the cost - effectiveness of using NUBs in CANs should be provided.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This manuscript proposes an approach coined "high activity & low content" to prepare CANs with high performance. The idea is to introduce only small percentage of fastly exchangeable bonds. the manuscript describes the behaviour of polyurethanes materials containing small fractions of active N-hydroxyphthalimide-urethanes bonds.
This manuscript does not bring much to the field of vitrimer. indeed the so called "high activity & low content" approach is not new. It is well known that decreasing the amount of exchangeable bonds will slow down the topological rearrangement and decrease creep and thus help maintain mechanical properties.
In addition, the authors do not present relevant reference materials to compare their materials to. for example the reference materials devoid of any N-hydroxyphthalimide-urethanes bonds are presented, although the reference thermoset and the reference thermoplastic version of their material would be very useful and reinforce the case the authors are trying to make.
Similarly, a systematic study of the effect of the crosslinking density woudl have been useful. indeed the crosslinking density varies from one material to teh other, but this is not clearly discussed( and the denomination of the aterials is misleading the percentage values annonced are actually not percentages).
There are also a few unsustantiated claims. for example the authors say: " Overall, these results demonstrate that the dynamic chemistry of NUBs is different from previously reported reversible isocyanate chemistry,32 and is characterized by a high degree of dissociation and a rapid association rate (large Kd and ka), which makes it possible to reprocess the corresponding CANs with a lower DCBs content." The authors do not prove at that stage that lower kinetics would not be sufficient to reprocess CAns acontaining low amonts of exchangeable bonds. and in effect , at that point in teh manuscriptn the authors have not proven yet that the CANs they propose are indeed CANs , and can be reprocessed.
The manusript is also not easy to follow since the actual formulation (and hence structural differences) as well as their main properties (Tg, Tdeg, Moduules etc...) are not tabulated in teh main text.
In the current state, I cannot recommend it for publication in Nature communications as the degree of novelty is questionnable, and the work lacks convincing benchmarking.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The manuscript “Minimal N-Hydroxyphthalimide-Urethane Bonds Enable Superior Thermomechanical Stability for Covalent Adaptable Networks” describes a well-design system of reversible isocyanate-based PUR with comparably high thermomechanical stability while being reprocessable. The manuscript is well structured and written, contributing to the field.
1. The design criteria to enable the comparably high thermomechanical stability for the PNUs are clearly communicated within the manuscript and is defined as “High activity & Low Content”. Have the authors considered the applicability of these criteria to other systems, for example by evaluating literature on CANs with low incorporation of dynamic bonds and compared their activity of association to this system and could the authors suggest other systems where these design criteria could or do apply? Such comparisons would contribute to the generality of the concept discussed. Upon revisions, the manuscript by Yin et.al. has been improved and many of the reviewer’s comments have been addressed and resolved. The answers and additional experiments however raise a new question, and there is one comment that has not been completely elucidated.
1. The authors are emphasizing their CAN design to be “high activity and low content”, meaning that a combination of an efficient thermal decomposition, and rapid association chemistry for dynamic covalent bonds in a low content, improves, for example, the mechanical properties. As this is suggested to be a novel design criterion, and the focus of the manuscript, it must be set in a larger context, where other dynamic chemistries and systems are included and compared (not only for PURs). Similar design criteria have been incorporated in other dynamic chemistries, although maybe not explicitly stated. This was highlighted by two of the reviewers in the first round of comments. The authors must compare the design criteria to other dynamic chemistries, showcasing the novelty of them in the larger context of all CANs. A suggestion is to focus on CANs where the “low content” concept is already satisfied. This would showcase the novelty of the concept, while simultaneously enabling the scientific community to broaden the concept.
2. The authors have now included hygrothermal aging experiments, which contributes to the understanding of the PNUs properties under use. The authors interpretation of the reduction in Youngs modulus, tensile strength and elongation-at-break is that it is a consequence of plasticization or alterations in microphase separation. Still, plasticization is commonly associated with a decrease in Tg and increase in elongation. As hygrothermal aging will be a key aspect for use, an elucidation of what is the prevailing mechanism would be of high interest. It also raises the question if there is an effect on properties at use conditions without elevated temperature. Performing the same experiment at room temperature with 100% humidity and also simply measuring if there are changes in properties as a function of time in room temperature with uncontrolled humidity would strengthen the study and possibly elucidate if plasticization or microstructure rearrangements dominate.
3. In table S8 and figure 3c, the authors compare elongation-at-break with toughness. As elongation contributes to toughness, would a clearer message be sent if elongation-at-break is compared to strength or strain-at-break for the materials?

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Compared to classic thermosets, the reprocessability of covalent adaptable networks (CANs) endowed by dynamic covalent bonds (DCBs) often comes at the expense of mechanical performance and thermomechanical stability. Herein, we report a “High Activity & Low Content” strategy for CANs to achieve superior thermomechanical stability, which is enabled by dynamic N-hydroxyphthalimide-urethane bonds (NUBs). The catalyst-free addition reaction between N-hydroxyphthalimides and isocyanates proceeds to an near-quantitative conversion within 2 h at room temperature in dimethyl sulfoxide, while the formed bonds dissociate even up to ~28% at 120 °C. The dual high activity, characterized by a high degree of dissociation and fast association kinetics, allows for an effective reduction in DCB content within CANs while preserving their dynamic characteristics. We incorporate only 5 mol% of dynamic units to develop poly(N-hydroxyphthalimide-urethanes) (PNU) networks. The “High Activity & Low Content” design endows PNUs with superior mechanical properties, exceptional crack tolerance, and remarkable mechanical stability at high temperatures. Furthermore, even with minimal DCB participation, the PNUs exhibit excellent reprocessability and mild degradability in neutral aqueous conditions. This study proposes a compelling strategy that enables CANs to achieve excellent reprocessability while retaining their mechanical strength and thermomechanical robustness—overcoming the traditional trade-off between these properties.

---

## Introduction

Thermosets with permanently crosslinked structures exhibit mechanical strength, solvent resistance, and durability, but also raise significant sustainability concerns1. Recent studies have reported innovative strategies to convert thermosets into reprocessable covalent adaptable networks (CANs) by incorporating dynamic covalent bonds (DCBs) such as transalkylation2,3, aza-Michael addition4, radical-mediated reaction5, disulfide/diselenide6, C=C/C=N metathesis7,8, nucleophilic aromatic substitution9. However, the developed CAN systems often face a fundamental trade-off: insufficient network dynamics reduce reprocessability, whereas excessive bond exchange degrades mechanical properties, especially the thermomechanical stability10–14. Consequently, it is a significant scientific challenge and practical imperative to pursue a delicate balance between mechanical stability and dynamic adaptability for the design of high-performance CANs.

The macroscopic behaviors of CANs are derived from the thermodynamic and kinetic parameters of DCBs governing the reconfiguration process and the mean lifetime of network crosslinks, as well as the macromolecular topology15–17. To avoid excessive flow of CANs at high temperatures, chemical approaches typically involve tailoring the kinetics of DCBs through trapping reactive counterparts18, developing DCBs with high activation energy barriers14, or introducing multiple types of dynamic bonds with disparate lifetimes, etc16,19–21. In parallel, topological design strategies include tuning cross-linking density22,23, and manipulating phase separation or nanoscale domains24,25 to optimize the balance between mechanical robustness and creep. Despite these significant advancements, most existing studies primarily focus on the service performance of CANs at low temperatures, where dynamic exchange reactions are sluggish or kinetically suppressed by limited polymer chain motion (<Tg or Tm)13,14,26. However, for demanding applications subject to high temperatures, such as thermal insulation and sealing, mechanical stability at elevated temperatures is important. We propose that a more general and straightforward strategy is to minimize the incorporation of dynamic bonds to mitigate the detrimental effects on material properties while enabling the reprocessing of as-formed CANs. For this purpose, DCBs must be carefully designed to satisfy two critical criteria: (i) efficient thermal dissociation (large dissociation equilibrium constant, Kd) at elevated temperatures to facilitate reprocessing, and (ii) rapid association reaction kinetics (large association rate constant, ka) at low temperatures to ensure complete network reformation at low DCB content (Fig. 1).

Reversible isocyanate chemistry, which focuses on the inherent reversibility of urethane/urea bonds, has garnered particular attention due to the diverse substrate structures available for modulating their dynamics1,27–31. This feature provides a promising candidate to meet the abovementioned stringent requirements. Isocyanates are highly reactive and usually react with active hydrogen compounds rapidly (large ka), which is typically accompanied by a substantial enthalpy change (large |ΔH|). Nevertheless, this usually results in a low degree of dissociation (low Kd, Fig. 1) at elevated temperatures27,32,33, as enthalpy changes typically dominate the overall Gibbs free energy change of a reaction. Therefore, developing a reversible chemistry that simultaneously exhibits both large Kd and ka remains challenging15,34.

Herein, we report a type of reversible isocyanate chemistry, N-hydroxyphthalimide-urethane bonds (NUBs), which enable concurrent high dissociability and fast reformation kinetics and demonstrate their efficacy in minimizing DCB content to enhance the mechanical properties and thermomechanical stability of the corresponding CANs. The dynamic chemistry of NUBs is controlled by the electronic effects of the phthalimide moiety in urethane. Specifically, the strong electron-withdrawing capability of the N-hydroxyphthalimide (NHPI) structure renders it a good leaving group5, thus promoting NUB dissociation with a conversion far higher than those of previously reported reversible isocyanate chemistry27,32,33. The high reactivity with isocyanates originates from the unique dipolar tautomer of NHPI, contributing to lowering the transition state activation energy. As a proof-of-concept, we have developed a series of poly(N-hydroxyphthalimide-urethanes) (PNUs) with a minimal proportion of NUBs (5 mol% of the total diisocyanate) as the dynamic building blocks. The resulting PNUs exhibit extraordinary tensile strength, toughness, and resistance to crack propagation, attributable to the reduction of dynamic weak bonds. This “High Activity & Low Content” design ensures thermal reprocessability and mild degradation while effectively maintaining thermomechanical stability of PNUs, as evidenced by excellent dimensional persistence, stress relaxation resistance, and network integrity at elevated temperatures. Consequently, the PNUs demonstrate significant potential as sustainable alternatives to conventional PUs, and this work provides a robust framework for manufacturing high-performance CANs by dynamic chemical design to overcome the traditional trade-off in dynamic networks.

---

## Results

Molecular dynamic chemistry
We first synthesized a series of model compounds (Supplementary Figs. S1–7, S37–48). The kinetics of the addition reaction between methoxy-NHPI(1) and hexyl isocyanate were investigated using in situ Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR). The sharp drop of the characteristic peak at 2276 cm–1, corresponding to the asymmetric stretching of the NCO group, implies the rapid formation of N-hydroxyphthalimide-urethane bonds in the absence of a catalyst (Fig. 2a, b). The formation reaction of NUBs exhibits first-order kinetics for both N-hydroxyl compounds and isocyanates (rate = ka[NOH][NCO]) (Supplementary Fig. S8), achieving ~ 97% conversion after approximately 2 h at room temperature with a large association rate constant of 1.3 × 10–2 M–1·s–1 in dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO). The association rate constant ka is comparable to previously reported oxime-urethane and pyrazole-urea bonds32,33. Interestingly, the reaction rate in N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF) dramatically decreased, but it is still much faster than that of conventional uncatalyzed urethane and thiourethane bonds (Fig. 2c and Supplementary Fig. S9)32,35. This phenomenon implies a distinct reaction mechanism for NUBs, since previously reported reversible isocyanate chemistries exhibit comparable reaction kinetics in these two solvents due to their similar hydrogen bonding abilities30,32,36.

Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were conducted to elucidate the mechanism of the addition reaction. The results revealed that NHPI can undergo an intramolecular 1,4-proton transfer (TS1) to form the 1,3-dipolar nitrone isomer (INT1), with an activation energy barrier of 20.5 kcal mol–1 (endergonic by 19.9 kcal mol–1). The nitrone subsequently may react with isocyanate via either a concerted or a stepwise mechanism. The concerted pathway begins with the formation of an isocyanate-nitrone complex (endergonic by 5.2 kcal mol–1) and is featured by the simultaneous hydrogen transfer and nucleophilic attack via a seven-membered ring transition state (TS2, ΔG≠=10.2 kcal mol–1), ultimately yielding the final product (endergonic by 24.1 kcal mol–1). The stepwise pathway in which nucleophilic attack precedes proton transfer is energetically unfavorable because the activation energy is approximately 12.2 kcal mol–1 higher than that of the concerted process. Additionally, theoretical calculations were performed for the direct addition between N-hydroxy and isocyanate via a concerted four-membered ring transition state, analogous to the typical reaction mechanism of isocyanates with alcohols. This pathway is ruled out for the disfavored activation energy barrier as high as 32.8 kcal mol–1 (Fig. 2d and Supplementary Figs. S10, S11). It’s worth noting that the favored reaction mechanism involves a thermodynamically unstable key intermediate, the 1,3-dipolar nitrone tautomer. Given that dipolar isomers (e.g., nitrones) typically exhibit enhanced stability in highly polar solvents (those with large dielectric constants (ε), like DMSO) due to the effective solvation and stabilization of the separated charges via dipole-dipole or ion-dipole interactions, this finding accounts for the remarkably accelerated reaction kinetics we observed in the order of DMSO > DMF > 1, 4-dioxane (εDMSO = 45 > εDMF = 36 > ε1,4-dioxane = 2)37,38.

Thermodynamic studies using in situ variable-temperature 1H NMR revealed that the NUB dissociated to NHPIs and isocyanates at elevated temperatures (Fig. 2e, f). The dissociation reaction reached equilibrium very rapidly in less than 20 min at 80 °C (Supplementary Figs. S12, S13). At 120 °C, the thermal dissociation ratio of NUB was up to 28%, with a dissociation equilibrium constant Kd of 2.72 × 10–2 M (Fig. 2f and Supplementary Table S1). Compared to oxime-urethane (Kd = 3.2 × 10–3 M), pyrazole-urea (Kd = 2.6 × 10–3 M), and imidazole-urea (Kd = 6.2 × 10–3 M, estimated by the Van’t Hoff equation)27,32,33, the dissociation ratio of the NUB endowed by the stronger electron-withdrawing NHPI group was much higher at the same temperature. Thermodynamically, the large dissociation equilibrium constant Kd is attributed to the small enthalpy change (ΔHd = 10.8 ± 0.7 kcal mol–1 from the Van’t Hoff plot) of the dissociation reaction (Fig. 2g, h). Subsequently, the reorganization was proved by the reversible recombination of the dissociated counterparts. When two model compounds, AB and CD, were mixed in anhydrous acetonitrile and heated at 80 °C, as expected, the formed exchange products CB and AD were successfully identified at about 10 min and 12 min by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) (Fig. 2i and Supplementary Fig. S14). Overall, these results demonstrate that the dynamic chemistry of NUBs is different from previously reported dynamic chemistry27,32,33,39–41, and is characterized by a high degree of dissociation and a rapid association rate (large Kd and ka, Supplementary Table S2).

Superior mechanical properties
Mechanical robustness is a prerequisite for CANs to meet the requirements of actual applications. Therefore, the mechanical deterioration associated with the incorporation of DCBs should be minimized as much as possible. With this in mind, we employed HDI, BDO as hard segments, PTMEG, Tri-NH2 as soft segments, and only a small amount (5 mol% relative to HDI) of bifunctional dynamic building blocks (Bi-NOH) to prepare a series of PNUs, denoted as PNU-A, PNU-B and PNU-C, with sequentially decreasing hard/soft segment ratios of 13/6.5, 12/7.5, 11/8.5 (Table 1, Figs. 1, 3a and Supplementary Figs. S15, S19, Table S3). Notably, the introduction of Bi-NOH did not significantly compromise the techno-economic feasibility (Supplementary Table S8). Swelling experiments conducted in different solvents verified that the gel fractions of PNUs remain above 95%, suggesting the well-defined crosslinked networks (Supplementary Fig. S20). Remarkably, PNU-A demonstrated a tensile strength of 43.2 ± 4.3 MPa, attaining an extraordinary elongation-at-break of 1891 ± 72% and a toughness of 404.4 MJ m-3, surpassing other covalently crosslinked dynamic PUs reported to date (Fig. 3b, c and Supplementary Fig. S21, Table S9)7–9,22,32,33,42–49. Their characteristic ‘J-shaped’ stress-strain curves indicated the advent of strain-induced crystallization (SIC) during stretching, a pivotal mechanism underpinning elastomer reinforcement. Consequently, the PNUs exhibited a pretty high true stress at break of up to 1.0 GPa, enabling a 5 kg weight to be lifted by 0.1 g PNU-A elastomer (Supplementary Fig. S22). In sequential cyclic tensile tests, the hysteresis loops increased significantly as the applied strain increased, indicating a progressive energy dissipation mechanism (Fig. 3d and Supplementary Fig. S23).

In addition to minimal incorporation of relatively weak NUBs, the aggregated structure of polymers also plays a crucial role in determining PNU performance. The carbonyl (C=O) stretching vibration regions (1800~1600 cm–1) in the FTIR spectra were deconvolved into multiple subpeaks, suggesting the presence of hierarchical hydrogen bonding. Quantitative analysis revealed that the content of hydrogen-bonded C=O in PNU-A was 73%, which is higher than that in PNU-B (69%) and PNU-C (39%) (Fig. 3e and Supplementary Fig. S24, Table S10). As the temperature increased from 30 to 160 °C, the spectral shifts such as ν(C=O), δ(N-H), ν(C-N) and ν(C-O-C) suggested the progressive dissociation of hydrogen bonds, which allows for effective energy dissipation under deformation (Fig. 3f). In situ stretching wide-angle X-ray scattering (WAXS) was performed to shed more light on the polymer morphology evolution during deformation. When unstretched, PNU-A showed concentric circles in the 2D WAXS spectra, typical of amorphous elastomers. As tensile strain increased, the pattern evolved from concentric circles to distinct spots (Fig. 3g and Supplementary Fig. S25). Concurrently, the broad hump in the 1D WAXS spectra became increasingly sharper, signifying enhanced chain alignment and increasingly ordered molecular packing (Fig. 3h). The underlying molecular mechanism involves the controlled release of soft segments composed of polyether chain segments during the initial stages of deformation. At large strains, the hard segments comprising the symmetric structure of HDI and the aromatic planarity of Bi-NOH withstand more stress and gradually align parallel to the tensile direction. This would facilitate crystallization and further reinforce PNUs (Fig. 3i). These evidences provide a mechanistic explanation for the pronounced nonlinear behavior observed in the stress-strain curves.

Exceptional crack tolerance
In addition to their remarkable ductility and toughness, the orientation of the abundant symmetric structure (from HDI) and aromatic planarity (from Bi-NOH) under deformation also empowers PNUs with exceptional crack tolerance. The PNU-A exhibited a fracture energy of 92.1 kJ m–2 (Fig. 4a), and a tear energy up to 460.1 kJ m–2 (Fig. 4b). In puncture resistance experiments, a 0.5 mm-radius needle tip penetrated a 0.2 mm-thick PNU-A film, yielding a puncture force of 13.2 N and a displacement of 11.2 mm (Fig. 4c). In situ stretching SEM was employed to elucidate the microscale crack growth behavior. A controlled displacement (Δd) was incrementally applied to a pre-cracked PNU-A specimen using an in situ stretching stage (Fig. 4d and Supplementary Fig. S26). During the initial deformation, SEM observations revealed rapid crack-tip blunting. As Δd increased, the crack underwent substantially transverse opening rather than propagating through the specimen. Notably, when Δd increased from 4.5 mm to 5.4 mm, the horizontal width at the narrowest section of the specimen decreased by only 0.077 mm, demonstrating strong resistance to crack advancement. At the final deformation stage, the cross-sectional area further decreased, and the specimen could no longer sustain the increasing applied load, triggering rapid flaw initiation and horizontal propagation, and ultimately resulting in catastrophic failure. Analysis of fracture morphology confirmed a significant deviation of the crack trajectory from its initial path (Fig. 4e, f). Digital image correlation (DIC) strain nephograms indicated that crack tip blunting efficiently alleviated stress concentration by redistributing localized stress to the surrounding region. This enabled the polymer chains near the crack tip to experience substantially greater vertical deformation, which activated SIC and led to significant reinforcement along the vertical axis, thereby inducing anisotropy within the material (Fig. 4g–i). Consequently, the crack tip no longer functioned as a stress concentration region in the horizontal direction, as vertical reinforcement effectively suppressed horizontal crack propagation.

Remarkable thermomechanical stability
To systematically investigate the influence of DCB content on the thermomechanical behavior of CANs, we synthesized two dynamic PNUs (PNU-15 mol% and PNU-30 mol%) alongside NUB-free reference thermoset (CPU) and thermoplastic (TPU) controls, all with the same hard/soft segment ratio as PNU-A (Table 1, Fig. 5a and Supplementary Figs. S15, S16, Table S4, S5). Tensile testing showed that the incorporation of NUBs with rigid ring structures endowed PNU-A with superior comprehensive mechanical properties compared to TPU and CPU. However, as the NUB content increased further, the mechanical response of the PNUs markedly changed from strong and tough to soft and weak, indicating that an overabundance of weak NUBs reduced the capacity of PNUs to withstand high loads and resistance to deformation (Fig. 5b).

Then, the mechanical behavior and dynamic properties at elevated temperatures were systematically evaluated. Dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) revealed a similar two-stage thermal transition in the storage modulus (E’), attributable to the distinct thermal transitions of the hard and soft segments. Notably, PNU-A retained a constant modulus plateau in the high-temperature region up to 160 °C, a characteristic also observed in CPU. This behavior suggested that the incorporation of a small fraction (5 mol%) of dynamic units minimally perturbed the integrity of the overall crosslinked network at high temperatures. However, at higher DCB contents, this plateau progressively evolved into a viscous-flow transition similar to TPU, featuring a continuously declining modulus (Fig. 5c, Supplementary Figs. S27, S28 and Table S11, S12). The temperature-strain curves quantitatively corroborated this trend. At lower temperatures, all PNUs deformed slowly with the same temperature dependency. Above 50 °C, however, strain increased suddenly, because of the softening of hard segments and the accelerated dissociation/exchange of DCBs. At 80 °C, the strain of PNU-A reached only ~9.0%, second to CPU (~4.1%), and much lower than PNU-15 mol% (~13.1%) and PNU-30 mol% (~20.9%) (Fig. 5d). Optical images further illustrated the dimensional stability at high temperatures: the triangular geometry of PNU-A was preserved upon heating, whereas PNU-30 mol% underwent pronounced viscous flow (Fig. 5e). Considering their similar transition temperatures from DMA, the poor dimensional stability is mainly due to the significant increase in network plasticity caused by dissociation of excessive DCBs.

The dynamic properties of networks were further studied by temperature-dependent stress relaxation experiments (Fig. 5f, g and Supplementary Fig. S29). As the temperature increased from 120 to 150 °C, the characteristic relaxation time (τ*) of PNU-A decreased from 4049 s to 339 s. In contrast, PNU-15 mol% and PNU-30 mol% exhibited notably shorter τ* even at 80 °C, reflecting accelerated network reorganization with increasing DCB content. In high-temperature time sweeps, PNU-A showed no discernible changes in storage (G’) and loss (G”) moduli over at least 60 min, indicating excellent thermomechanical stability of PNUs upon heating (Fig. 5h). Frequency sweeps revealed that PNU-A maintained a stable crosslinked network, similar to CPU, with its G’ consistently exceeding G” and both moduli remaining temperature-insensitive at 100~140 °C. In contrast, the network of PNU-15 mol% was much more susceptible to heat, resulting in a pronounced reduction in its modulus. Strikingly, PNU-30 mol% displayed a G’/G” crossover at a lower temperature of 100 °C, indicative of a transition to a viscous-flow dominant state (Fig. 5i–k and Supplementary Fig. S30). Additionally, PNUs with a minimal NUBs exhibit comparable hygrothermal aging resistance to the CPU (Supplementary Fig. S31 and Table S13). Taken together, these results fully reflect that the “High Activity & Low Content” design preserves an integrated network with a high-temperature mechanical stability, which is significant for high-temperature applications of CANs, while still enabling dynamic adaptability.

Reprocessability and mild degradability
Arrhenius analysis revealed that the PNUs with varying hard/soft segment ratios exhibited similar stress relaxation activation energies of 23.9~26.9 kcal mol–1, suggesting that the plasticity of these networks is governed by the rearrangement of NUBs. Due to the high dissociation and the rapid reformation of the NUBs, PNUs containing only 5 mol% DCB could be efficiently hot pressed at 140 °C under 10 MPa for 30 min (Fig. 6a, b). Tensile tests revealed that the PNUs containing 5 mol% NUBs retained nearly unchanged tensile strength and elongation at break after repeated reprocessing, whereas both poly(oxime-urethane) (POU) containing 5 mol% oxime-urethane bonds with a relatively low degree of dissociation (12% at 120 °C vs. 28% at 120 °C for NUBs) and CPU (without NUBs) exhibit poor reprocessability and pronounced deterioration due to insufficient topological rearrangement (Table 1, Fig. 6c–e and Supplementary Table S6, Figs. S17, S32, S33). These results demonstrate that our “High activity & Low content” strategy strikes a balance between efficient network rearrangement and mechanical retention.

In addition to thermal reprocessability, we achieved degradation of PNUs under mild natural aqueous conditions and direct reuse of the degradation products. Urethane bonds are intrinsically stable, so the conventional chemical recycling of PU usually requires harsh conditions such as high temperature, acids/bases, or catalysts1,50,51. In contrast, our strategy exploited the high thermal dissociation tendency of NUBs and captured the generated isocyanates with water, thereby irreversibly shifting the equilibrium toward dissociation under mild conditions (Fig. 6f). Model experiments showed that the NUBs dissociated into NHPIs and isocyanates, with the latter subsequently reacting with water to form urea. This process was evidenced by a urea N-H proton appearing at δ 5.73 ppm in the 1H NMR spectrum, alongside an exchangeable proton at δ 10.80 ppm attributable to the N-hydroxy compound. At 100 °C, nearly complete degradation was attained after 8 h (Fig. 6g and Supplementary Fig. S34). Guided by this insight, the linear PNU-D bearing NUBs (Supplementary Fig. S18, Table S7) were prepared and then degraded in DMF containing 10% water at 100 °C. After 3 days, the weight-average molecular weight (Mw) of the PNU-D decreased from 50.0 kDa to 22.2 kDa (Fig. 6h). The resulting oligomers, enriched with polar groups (urea and urethane), were directly repurposed as adhesives. They demonstrated robust adhesion to diverse substrates via hydrogen bonding or coordination interactions (Fig. 6i, j and Supplementary Fig. S35, S36). These investigations provided valuable insights for designing reprocessable and degradable polymers by skillfully employing dual-active NUBs.

---

## Methods

Synthesis of the crosslinked PNUs
Typical procedure: polyols (e.g., BDO, PTMEG) were vacuum dehydrated for 12 h before use, and the flasks were dried in a vacuum oven at 120 °C. HDI (10 equiv., 30 mmol, 5.046 g) and Bi-NOH (0.5 equiv., 1.5 mmol, 0.510 g) were dissolved in 30 mL anhydrous DMF, and the mixture was stirred overnight at room temperature under N2 atmosphere. Then PTMEG (5.5 equiv., 16.5 mmol, 16.500 g), BDO (2.5 equiv., 7.5 mmol, 0.676 g), and DBTDL (0.030 g) were added, and the solution was mechanically stirred at 80 °C for 3 h under N2 atmosphere. The reaction system was then diluted with 100 mL anhydrous 1,4-dioxane and cooled to room temperature. Tri-NH2 (1 equiv., 3 mmol, 1.320 g) dissolved in 10 mL anhydrous 1,4-dioxane was slowly added to the reaction solution under vigorous stirring, followed by a rapid increase in viscosity and gelation. The prepared PNU gels were placed in a fume hood to evaporate the solvent at room temperature for 24 h and then placed in a vacuum oven at 60 °C for 12 h to remove the residual solvent.

Synthesis of the reference TPU and CPU
TPU procedure: polyols (e.g., BDO, PTMEG) were vacuum dehydrated for 12 h before use, and the flasks were dried in a vacuum oven at 120 °C. HDI (10 equiv., 30 mmol, 5.046 g), PTMEG (7 equiv., 21 mmol, 21.000 g), BDO (3 equiv., 9 mmol, 0.811 g), and DBTDL (0.030 g) were dissolved in 30 mL anhydrous DMF, and the mixture was mechanically stirred at 80 °C for 3 h under N2 atmosphere. The prepared TPU was placed in a fume hood to evaporate the solvent at room temperature for 24 h and then placed in a vacuum oven at 60 °C for 12 h to remove the residual solvent.

CPU procedure: polyols (e.g., BDO, PTMEG) were vacuum dehydrated for 12 h before use, and the flasks were dried in a vacuum oven at 120 °C. HDI (10 equiv., 30 mmol, 5.046 g), PTMEG (5.5 equiv., 16.5 mmol, 16.500 g), BDO (3 equiv., 9 mmol, 0.811 g,) and DBTDL (0.030 g) were dissolved in 30 mL anhydrous DMF, and the mixture was mechanically stirred at 80 °C for 3 h under N2 atmosphere. The reaction system was then diluted with 100 mL anhydrous 1,4-dioxane and cooled to room temperature. Tri-NH2 (1 equiv., 3 mmol, 1.320 g) dissolved in 10 mL anhydrous 1,4-dioxane was slowly added to the reaction solution under vigorous stirring, followed by a rapid increase in viscosity and gelation. The prepared CPU gel was placed in a fume hood to evaporate the solvent at room temperature for 24 h and then placed in a vacuum oven at 60 °C for 12 h to remove the residual solvent.

Synthesis of the reference POU
The synthesis procedure for POU was analogous to that for crosslinked PNUs. In the formulation, Bi-NOH (0.5 equiv., 1.5 mmol, 0.510 g) was replaced by dimethylglyoxime (0.5 equiv., 1.5 mmol, 0.174). All other steps remained identical.

Synthesis of the linear PNU (PNU-D)
PEG was vacuum dehydrated for 12 h before use, and the flasks were dried in a vacuum oven at 120 °C. HDI (10 equiv., 30 mmol, 5.046 g) and Bi-NOH (1 equiv., 3 mmol, 1.021 g) were dissolved in 30 mL anhydrous DMF, and the sealed mixture was stirred overnight at room temperature. After adding PEG (9 equiv., 27 mmol, 27.000 g) and DBTDL (0.030 g), the solution was mechanically stirred at 80 °C for 3 h under a N2 atmosphere.

Reprocessing of the crosslinked PUs
Reprocessing experiments were carried out by hot pressing. The specimens were sectioned into small pieces and subsequently hot pressed within a rectangular mold at 120 °C or 140 °C under 10 MPa for 30 min. After cooling to room temperature, the reprocessed samples (recycle 1) were demolded and then cut into dumbbell-shaped specimens for uniaxial tensile measurements, as well as rectangular specimens for DMA. The recycle 1 specimens were reprocessed repeatedly following the abovementioned procedure to obtain recycle 2, recycle 3, and recycle 4 specimens, respectively.

Mild degradation of PNU-D
The chemical degradation mechanism of NUBs was investigated by 1H NMR using the model compound (CD). CD (0.384 g, 1.2 mmol) and 324 µL of H2O (18 mmol) were added into DMSO-d6 to prepare a 0.2 M solution. The mixture was then stirred at different temperatures, and samples were taken out at different periods for 1H NMR (Supplementary Fig. S21). Upon heating, CD dissociated into 1 and 2, and the latter reacted irreversibly with water to form the transient 3, which was consumed by the next dissociated 2 to form 4 with a urea structure, contributing to a continuous shift of the chemical equilibrium of CD in the direction of dissociation. The percentage of degradation was determined by the integral ratio of b (belonging to the starting compound CD) and b’ (belonging to the degradation product 4).

We then investigated the degradation of PNU-D bearing the NUBs (Supplementary Table S6).
